nameStory: The name "bladderwort" comes from the tiny bladder-like traps hidden underwater on the plant's submerged stems. These microscopic bladders work like vacuum pumps, sucking in tiny water creatures for food! The scientific name "tenuicaulis" means "slender stem," describing this species' particularly delicate underwater structure.
description: Slender-stemmed bladderwort is a rare aquatic carnivorous plant that floats just below the water's surface in quiet ponds and wetlands. Like other bladderworts, it has no true roots, instead drifting freely with thread-like underwater stems that bear tiny bladder traps. Above water, it sends up delicate flower stalks with small yellow snapdragon-like blooms. This is one of New England's rarest bladderworts, found in only a handful of locations.

idTips.label: Underwater Stems
idTips.description: Extremely fine, thread-like submerged stems that feel almost hair-like when you gently run them through your fingers - much more delicate than other bladderworts

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers shaped like tiny snapdragons with a lower lip and small spur, rising 2-4 inches above the water on thin stalks

idTips.label: Bladder Traps
idTips.description: Microscopic clear bladders scattered along the underwater stems - you'll need a magnifying glass to see these tiny vacuum traps clearly

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Free-floating with no roots, drifting just below the surface like a submerged spider web of incredibly fine stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, highly divided underwater leaf segments that are so fine they're barely visible - much more reduced than most bladderworts

habitat: Found in quiet, shallow ponds, bog pools, and slow-moving waters with soft, acidic conditions. Prefers nutrient-poor waters in sphagnum bogs and marshy areas where competition from other aquatic plants is limited. Often associated with other carnivorous plants like sundews and pitcher plants in specialized wetland communities.

seasonality.spring: Underwater stems begin active growth as water warms, though the plant may be present year-round in ice-free areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with small yellow flowers appearing above the water surface from June through August, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants may form winter buds (turions) that sink to the bottom to overwinter.
seasonality.winter: Plants typically dormant as winter buds on the pond bottom, with no visible above-water parts in frozen habitats.

funFact: Each tiny bladder trap can suck in a water flea in less than a millisecond - faster than you can blink! The plant creates a vacuum inside each bladder, and when tiny hairs are triggered, a trap door opens and whoosh - dinner is served in one of nature's speediest hunting techniques.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other bladderworts, but the extremely fine, hair-like underwater stems are distinctive. If the submerged parts look substantial enough to easily grab with your fingers, it's probably a different bladderwort species. Remember: slender-stemmed bladderwort lives up to its name with remarkably delicate underwater growth.
contextualKnowledge: This species is so rare in New England that many botanists go their entire careers without seeing it. With only 6 recorded observations, finding one would be like discovering a botanical treasure. The extreme rarity makes positive identification especially important for conservation efforts.
compareHints: Distinguished from common bladderwort by much finer, more delicate underwater stems and smaller overall size. Unlike purple bladderwort which has more robust purple flowers, this species has typical yellow bladderwort blooms. The thread-like stems separate it from swollen bladderwort, which has inflated floating structures, and from horned bladderwort, which grows in wet soil rather than floating freely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horned bladderwort stands out from its many bladderwort relatives by having the most prominent horn-like spur and by growing in terrestrial or semi-aquatic conditions rather than fully underwater.
Small swollen bladderwort is smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort and lacks the large inflated floats of swollen bladderwort.
Among New England's bladderworts, purple bladderwort is unique for its purple flowers – most others have yellow blooms.
Common bladderwort is the largest and most robust of New England's bladderworts, with the biggest flowers and most substantial underwater growth.
Swollen bladderwort is the largest of New England's aquatic bladderworts and the only one with truly prominent inflated stems that feel spongy to the touch.
Intermediate bladderwort differs from common bladderwort by having fewer, slightly smaller flowers and more delicate overall appearance.
Humped bladderwort is much smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort, forming thin surface mats rather than robust underwater colonies.
Northeastern bladderwort is distinguished from other New England bladderworts by its lavender-purple flowers and preference for very shallow water or bog margins.

Hidden-fruit Bladderwort is unique among New England's bladderworts for keeping its flowers at or below the water surface, while most relatives like Common and Purple Bladderwort hold their blooms well above water on conspicuous stalks.
Lesser bladderwort is distinguished from common bladderwort by its much smaller size and more delicate appearance overall.
Among New England's bladderworts, zigzag bladderwort is unique for its terrestrial zigzag growth habit - most other bladderworts either float in water or grow upright from water.
